messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Thea

Thea was thirty-five when she came to her first appointment, her hands steady as she filled out the intake forms but her jaw clenched tight enough that the therapist noticed. She was a physical therapist herself—worked at a clinic in Portland, Oregon, specializing in post-operative rehabilitation—and she moved through the waiting room with the composed efficiency of someone trained to manage pain in others. What she did not say in the waiting room, but would say within the hour, was that she could no longer touch her patients without her hands trembling.

The event had happened four years ago. Thea had been married to Marcus for six years at that point, and the relationship had been deteriorating in ways she had not fully admitted to herself until the night it became impossible to deny. They had been arguing about money—about her working too much, about his unemployment, about the shape their life had taken—and the argument had moved from the kitchen to the bedroom. Marcus had grabbed her wrist, hard enough that she felt the bone shift. When she tried to pull away, he had forced her onto the bed, and what happened next existed in her memory not as a sequence of moments but as a kind of eternal present tense, a sensation that would not resolve into past.

She remembered the specific temperature of his hands on her skin—cold, deliberately cold because he had held them under the bathroom faucet first, and she understood later that this was intentional, that the cold was part of the control. She remembered being unable to move her legs because he was sitting on them. She remembered saying no, and him saying that she had made him do this, that she had pushed him to it, and believing, in the moment and for a long time after, that this might be true.

They had stayed married for another year. Thea had not told anyone what happened. She had gone to work, treated patients, moved through her days as though the person she had been before—the woman who could touch another human being without fear—still existed. But by the time she finally left Marcus, that woman was already gone.

Now, four years later, Thea found herself unable to work. The problem was not dramatic or obvious. She could still perform the technical aspects of her job. But when a patient came in for a shoulder assessment, and she moved her hands toward their neck to palpate the trapezius, her body would flood with something that felt like the memory was happening again—not as something she was remembering, but as something that was occurring in real time. The temperature of her own hands would suddenly feel wrong, or she would become aware of her patient's trust in her, their vulnerability, and she would become convinced that something was fundamentally broken in her, that she was dangerous, that her presence in the room was a threat even though she knew rationally this made no sense.

She had started finding reasons to delegate the hands-on work. She told her supervisor she was developing carpal tunnel. She suggested patients see her colleagues instead. Within six months, her caseload had shrunk by half. Her supervisor had pulled her aside and asked if everything was all right. Thea had not known how to answer.

The intrusive memories had worsened over the past year. She would be lying in bed next to her current husband, David—a kind man, careful with her, whom she had married two years ago—and suddenly she would be back in that bedroom, and the feeling of being trapped, of having no choice, would be so overwhelming that she would have to get up and leave. David had stopped trying to touch her without explicit permission. He had stopped trying to understand why.

What frightened Thea most was the thought that Marcus had been right, that something in the way she was had invited what happened, that the defect was hers and not circumstantial. She spent hours thinking about what she might have said differently that night, what she might have done. She would replay the argument in her mind, searching for the moment where she could have prevented it all, and the searching never ended because there was no moment where prevention became possible once the violence had already begun. Yet she searched anyway, convinced that if she could only find the right version of that night, she could undo not just the event but the person she had become—the woman who flinches at temperature changes, who cannot allow herself to be touched, who no longer recognizes herself in the mirror and believes she never will again.

It was David who had finally insisted she see someone. He had said it gently, without blame, but with a kind of quiet firmness that she recognized as love. Thea had agreed, though she was not sure what she hoped would happen. She was not sure she deserved to feel better.
